'''''Guaiacum sanctum''''', commonly known as '''holywood''', '''lignum vitae'''<ref name=:2 /> or '''holywood lignum-vitae''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Larrea tridentata|creosote bush]] family, [[Zygophyllaceae]]. It is native to the [[Neotropical realm]], from Mexico through Central America, Florida in the United States, the [[Caribbean]], and northern South America.<ref>[https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=18048 U.S. National Plant Germplasm System]</ref> It has been introduced to other tropical areas of the world. It is currently threatened by [[habitat loss]] in its native region, and as such, is currently rated [[near threatened]] on the [[IUCN Red List]].
''Guaiacum sanctum'' is the [[National emblem|national tree]] of the Bahamas.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |url=http://thebahamasguide.com/facts/national-symbols/ |title=National Symbols of the Bahamas |work=Bahamas Facts and Figures |publisher=TheBahamasGuide |access-date=27 January 2009 }}</ref>

== Etymology ==
The native [[Taíno]] of the Caribbean referred to the tree as '''guayacán'''.<ref>{{cite web |last=Dr. Coll Y Toste |first=Cayetano |title=Diccionario Indígena |url=http://www.proyectosalonhogar.com/enciclopedia_ilustrada/Diccionario1.htm |work=Enciclopedia Clásicos de Puerto Rico |publisher=Real Academia de la Historia |location=Barcelona, Spain |edition=2nd |publication-date=1972 |language=es }}</ref> The common English name is a direct translation of the Spanish "palo santo" (not to be confused with ''[[Bursera graveolens]]''). [[Francisco López de Gómara]] as well as [[Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés|Oviedo]] make reference to the specific species as such in their respective histories of the New World. It earned its name during the time of the Spanish conquest of the New World for its use treating [[syphilis]], whose effects recalled the "evil" of the Black Death. Its scientific name is a Latinization of the Taíno ''guayacán'' as well as the word ''sanctum'', meaning holy.

==Properties==
This small tree is slow-growing, reaching about {{cvt|7|m|ft}} in height with a trunk diameter of {{cvt|50|cm|in}}. The tree is essentially [[evergreen]] throughout most of its native range. It is shade-tolerant. It fruits between the age of 30 and 70 years over the summer months in the Northern Hemisphere.<ref name="GRIN"/>

The wood is hard, heavy and self-lubricating, and has a [[Janka hardness test|Janka Hardness Score]] of 4500,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Friedrich |first1=K |last2=Akpan |first2=E |last3=Wetzel |first3=B |title=Structure and mechanical/abrasive wear behavior of a purely natural composite: black-fiber palm wood |journal=Journal of Materials Science |volume=52 |issue=17 |pages=10217–10229 |date=16 May 2017 |bibcode=2017JMatS..5210217F |s2cid=136327944 |doi=10.1007/s10853-017-1184-5 }}</ref> which is one of the hardest in the world. It can sink when placed in water.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.usanpn.org/nn/Guaiacum_sanctum |title=''Guaiacum sanctum'' |work=Nature's Notebook |publisher=National Phenology Network |access-date=15 April 2018 }}</ref> There are fine ripple marks on the wood.<ref>Record, Samuel J. "Tier-Like Arrangement of the Elements of Certain Woods." ''Science'', vol. 35, no. 889, 1912, pp. 75–77. ''JSTOR'', JSTOR, www.jstor.org/stable/1638125.</ref> [[File:Guaiacum sanctum 12zz.jpg|thumb|right|Leaves]]

===Leaves===
The [[leaves]] are [[Compound leaf|compound]], {{cvt|2.5|-|3|cm|in|1}} in length, and {{cvt|2|cm|in|1}} wide. They are dark green in color and occur as three to five pairs of [[leaflet (botany)|leaflet]]s.<ref name=":2">{{cite web |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=287642&isprofile=0& |title=''Guaiacum sanctum'' |website=Plant Finder |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |language=en-US |access-date=16 April 2018 }}</ref> They fold together during the hottest parts of the day.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Holywood lignum vitae (''Guaiacum sanctum'') |url=https://www.arkive.org/holywood-lignum-vitae/guaiacum-sanctum/image-G73445.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150921013429/http://www.arkive.org/holywood-lignum-vitae/guaiacum-sanctum/image-G73445.html |archive-date=21 September 2015 |website=Wildscreen Arkive |publisher=Wildscreem |access-date=15 April 2018 }}</ref>

===Flower===
The purplish blue [[flower]]s have five [[petal]]s each. They can grow individually or in clusters at the ends of branches.<ref name=":0" /> The flowers have both male and female parts ([[stamen]]s and [[pistil]]s) and yield yellow pods containing black [[seed]]s encapsulated separately in a red skin.<ref name=":3">{{cite book |last=Stubbins |first=Mark |title=Flowering Trees of Florida |publisher=Pineapple Press |location=Florida, USA |year=1999 |pages=78–81 }}</ref> [[File:Guaiacum sanctum-Artz.jpg|thumb|right|Flower]] [[File:Guaiacum sanctum—seed pods Photo by Katherine Wagner-Reiss 02.jpg|thumb|right|Seed pods open to reveal red arils]]

==Uses==
{{for|more uses of the wood|Lignum vitae}}
This tree is one of two species that yield the valuable [[lignum vitae]] wood, the other being ''[[Guaiacum officinale]]''.

The wood has been used for making specific parts of ships that needed to be self-lubricating so that they would last longer.

The tree is considered to have medicinal value, used mostly for [[traditional medicine|home remedies]]. The naturalist [[William Turner (naturalist)|William Turner]] noted in 1568 that the plant was already being grown in India, [[Tamraparni]] (ancient Sri Lanka), Java and the Tivu islets of the ocean, and whose [[broth]] cured several harsh diseases, including French pox ([[syphilis]]).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Turner |first1=William |title=William Turner: A New Herball: Parts II and III |date=1995 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-44549-8 |page=670 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ouWABJeOC4MC&q=taprobane+diet&pg=PA742 |access-date=14 June 2019 }}</ref><ref>Munger, Robert S. "Guaiacum, the Holy Wood from the New World". ''Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences'', vol. 4, no. 2, 1949, pp. 196–229. ''JSTOR'', JSTOR, www.jstor.org/stable/24619141.</ref> The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] can be [[steeped]] to create tonics.<ref name=":1" />
It is also used as an [[ornamental plant]].<ref name=":2" />

==Threats==
The type of rainforest ([[Tropical and subtropical dry broadleaf forests|tropical-deciduous and dry forests]]) that holywood is found in are the most threatened ecosystems in the world.<ref name="GRIN" /> The [[IUCN Red List]] considers the species [[Near-threatened species|Near Threatened]], while [[NatureServe conservation status|NatureServe]] considers the Florida population (which is limited to the [[Florida Keys]] and [[Miami-Dade County, Florida|Miami-Dade County]]) to be ''Critically Imperiled''.<ref name="TNC"/> It is possibly [[extirpated]] from El Salvador.

The plant was exploited until it was [[Endangered species|endangered]] due to use for [[Lumber|timber]] and [[Resin|medical resin]]. [[Deforestation]] also occurred to create more human-managed areas like farmland, cities, etc.<ref name="GRIN" /> This has caused [[habitat fragmentation]] for the species, which reduces the chances of lowering its risk status.<ref>Eric J. Fuchs, James L. Hamrick; Genetic Diversity in the Endangered Tropical Tree, ''Guaiacum sanctum'' (Zygophyllaceae), ''Journal of Heredity'', Volume 101, Issue 3, 1 May 2010, Pages 284–291, {{doi|10.1093/jhered/esp127 }}</ref> Moreover, since this is a slow-growing tree, it becomes harder to regrow and maintain sizable forests of it. It can be cultivated to grow faster, but needs to be watered regularly and to have [[Drainage|well-drained soil]].<ref name=":3" />

It has no major [[Pest (organism)|pests]]<ref name=":3" /> and though there were cases of illegal trade in 2008, this is no longer a major threat to the species.<ref name="GRIN" />
